domains.title: Great Thing Lord of Mount Miwa
domains.subtitle: Mountain, Oracle, and Sacred Snake
domains.lead: Ōmononushi is the mysterious kami of Mount Miwa, one of the oldest and most enigmatic deities in Japan. He is associated with snakes, oracles, and the transfer of the land to Amaterasu's descendants. Unlike most kami, he had no image and was worshipped in the form of the mountain itself.

cards.name: Mountain God
cards.desc: He is identified with Mount Miwa itself; Ōmiwa Shrine has no inner sanctuary because the peak is the kami's body.

cards.name: Snake Deity
cards.desc: He comes to Ikutamayori as a serpent in the Kojiki, and snake offerings of sake attend his Miwa cult.

cards.name: Oracle Kami
cards.desc: His consent to the land-transfer was given by oracle — sovereignty in Japan changes hands by consultation, not conquest.

cards.name: Land Transfer
cards.desc: He is the voice that yields the land to the heavenly descendants, binding the Miwa line to the imperial house.

symbols.name: Mount Miwa

symbols.name: Sake

symbols.name: The Miwa-torii
symbols.meaning: The unique three-pillared torii through which worshippers face the peak directly — architecture that frames a god who is geology

mythology.lead: Ōmononushi's mythology is preserved in strange, archaic tales of snakes, possession, and oracles — the Kojiki's strangest marriage, the constitution of Japan's sovereignty, and a shrine with no god-house, because the mountain is the god.

myths.title: The Serpent Husband of Ikutamayori
myths.text:
A maiden named Ikutamayori was visited each night by a beautiful man who came unseen. When she bore his child, her parents demanded to know the father. She had him leave a needle threaded with red silk in the hem of his garment; in the morning she followed the thread, and it led to the foot of Mount Miwa and vanished into a cave — where the visitor declared himself: he was Ōmononushi, the great lord of the mountain, and he appeared in serpent form. The child of this union was Kotoshironushi, the god who would one day counsel the peaceful surrender of the land to the heavenly grandson (Kojiki; cf. Nihon Shoki, Aston's translation).

The tale binds three things into one knot — mountain, snake, and the Miwa priestly line, whose descent from the kami's human bride it exists to explain.

myths.title: The Oracle of the Land
myths.text:
When the heavenly emissary Takemikazuchi descended to demand the land from the earthly god Ōnamuji (Ōkuninushi), Ōnamuji consulted his children. Kotoshironushi, away at Cape Miwa, answered that resistance to the heavenly grandson was hopeless — and then all eyes turned to the mountain. Ōmononushi was consulted, and his oracle settled the matter: 'Let the land be given over in peace,' he declared; the land was yielded, and he withdrew into a hidden realm, promising that his favor would attend his proper worship. The Nihon Shoki tells the same event differently, folding the mountain god into Ōnamuji himself: Ōnamuji, it says, is also called Ōmononushi (Kojiki; Nihon Shoki, tr. Aston, I).

Here the god is pure voice: sovereignty changes hands in Japan not by conquest but by consultation — and the mountain kami's consent is the constitution.

myths.title: The Bride of Miwa
myths.text:
Ōmononushi took as wife Seyadatarahime, daughter of his own son Kotoshironushi by Ikutamayori — and their child was the princess Himetataraisuzuhime. She became the consort of Emperor Sujin and bore the future Emperor Suinin: the serpent-god of Mount Miwa thus entered the imperial genealogy itself, the god's line becoming grandmother to the next sovereign. The Kojiki's genealogy is compressed and the texts do not spell every step out plainly, but the dynastic point stands: the mountain married into the house that received the mountain's realm.

The marriage also sealed an alliance between the Miwa priestly house and the court — the god who gave the land away kept his blood beside the throne. The Kojiki records the whole sequence without wonder, as plain genealogy: which is how one knows the text was compiled on the winning side.

myths.title: The Plague and the Possessed Princess
myths.text:
In Emperor Sujin's reign plague and disaster struck the land, and divination named the cause: the great kami of Mount Miwa, never yet given a shrine, was angry. The god made his will known by possessing a princess of his own line and speaking through her: worship me, he demanded, and I will cause the land to flourish. Sujin founded the rites; the pestilence lifted. The Nihon Shoki's parallel account likewise has the god speak through a human mouth, claim credit for guiding the cession of the land, and demand his due — the god of Miwa and the god of the land-transfer asserted as one and the same (Kojiki; Nihon Shoki, Aston I).

Myth here explains a liturgy: Ōmiwa's worship began, the texts insist, when the neglected mountain finally raised its voice.

myths.title: Worship without Image
myths.text:
Ōmiwa Shrine, at the foot of the mountain in Nara prefecture, is one of Japan's oldest shrines and one of the strangest: it has no honden, no inner sanctuary housing a divine image, because the god is not symbolized by anything — the god is Mount Miwa. Worshippers pray toward the peak across a unique three-pillared torii, the Miwa-torii; before the worship hall stand sacred sake casks, for Ōmononushi is patron of the brewers of Miwa, and his serpent form — a great snake said to coil in the mountain's caves — was traditionally offered sake. First listed among the great shrines in the Engishiki (927 CE), the site preserves a stratum of Japanese religion older than images: the mountain itself as shintai, the deity's body.

The absent statue is the theology: what has no face cannot be owned, and what cannot be owned cannot be conquered.

lore.syncretism: Ōmononushi never left Shinto, but he was folded into it from two directions. The Nihon Shoki already identifies him with Ōkuninushi — the local Miwa kami gathered into the imperial land-myth — and medieval honji suijaku doctrine went further: Mount Miwa's deity, as Miwa Daimyōjin, was given the Buddhist original ground of Śākyamuni Buddha, and Miwa mandalas picture the mountain with Buddhist cosmography laid over it. Under the mountain, ascetics of the Shugendō tradition practiced until the modern period, treating the peak itself as the object of cult. The serpent, the sake, and the oracle — archaic, local, and oracular — are precisely the features a centralizing mythology needed to absorb rather than erase: Ōmononushi survives because he was useful, first to the court that took his oracle, then to the Buddhism that crowned him, then to the brewers who still hang cedar balls for him.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ōmiwa Shrine still stands where the myth says it must: at the foot of Mount Miwa, without a main hall, prayer aimed at the peak. The surrounding district remains sacred geography — Isonokami, one of Japan's oldest shrines, close by, and the great early kofun of Hashihaka on the horizon. Miwa sake is still brewed under the god's patronage, and brewers across Japan hang sugitama cedar balls in his honor. The mountain appears in Nara-period poetry, and the Miwa-torii's third pillar is studied wherever shrine architecture is taught. For modern Shinto, Ōmononushi is the standing proof that the kami need not be anthropomorphic: his 'image' is a modest ridge of green rock and cedar, and on clear mornings the faithful still bow toward it before entering the shrine.
lore.extendedMeditation: Ōmononushi is the god who refuses to be a person. Every other great kami of Japan acquired a face, a genealogy, a palace in the poems; Ōmononushi acquired a mountain, and the mountain — unportable, unburnable, unshippable — has guarded his integrity ever since. He enters myth only as a voice or a snake: the two forms in which the sacred appears without becoming an idol. His oracle teaches a politics as well: the land changed hands because he consented, and consent, not conquest, is what his cult claims as the first principle of sovereignty. Even his marriage reads like an essay in legitimacy, wedding the mountain's line to the dynasty that received the mountain's realm. And because there is no statue, every visit to Ōmiwa is a small reenactment of the discovery of the sacred — you look up from the torii, past the sake casks, at green rock and cedar, and understand that you have been inside the shrine since the road.
lore.archaeology: The Engishiki shrine register (927 CE) already lists Ōmiwa among the great sanctuaries, and the site's archaeology is deep: excavations around Miwa have yielded ritual deposits and prestige objects — bronze mirrors, swords, and beads — from the Yayoi-to-Kofun transition, indicating a sanctuary of unusual antiquity at the mountain's foot, and the great keyhole tomb Hashihaka nearby marks the district as an early center of power. No honden has ever stood at Ōmiwa; worship runs toward the peak through the unique Miwa-torii, whose third central pillar frames the mountain as the true sanctuary. The 'artifact' of this god is thus geological and botanical at once — bedrock, cedar, and the spring-water sake that the shrine has brewed since the rite began.
